body.en: Advanced ACT Math (Subject Test Level 1) elevates number theory far beyond elementary arithmetic. Problems test divisibility proofs, greatest common divisors, least common multiples, modular congruence, cyclicity of powers, and convergence of geometric series.

label.en: Definition 1.1 — Divisibility, Prime Factorization, and GCD / LCM

body.en:
Fundamental properties of integers \(\mathbb{Z}\):
  • Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic: Every integer \(n > 1\) can be uniquely represented as a product of prime powers:
    \[ n = p_1^{e_1} p_2^{e_2} \cdots p_k^{e_k} \]
  • GCD and LCM Product Duality: For any positive integers \(a\) and \(b\):
    \[ \gcd(a, b) \cdot \text{lcm}(a, b) = a \cdot b \]Taking prime powers \(a = \prod p_i^{a_i}\) and \(b = \prod p_i^{b_i}\):
    \[ \gcd(a, b) = \prod p_i^{\min(a_i, b_i)}, \qquad \text{lcm}(a, b) = \prod p_i^{\max(a_i, b_i)} \]
  • Divisibility Tests:
    An integer is divisible by \(3\) (or \(9\)) iff the sum of its digits is divisible by \(3\) (or \(9\)).
    An integer is divisible by \(4\) iff its last two digits form a multiple of \(4\); by \(8\) iff its last three digits form a multiple of \(8\).
    An integer is divisible by \(11\) iff the alternating sum of its digits is a multiple of \(11\).

label.en: ● Deep Conceptual Intuition — Advanced Number Theory

body.en: Proportional Invariance, Linear Structure & Quantitative Modeling: Across ACT International Subject Test — Math 1, multi-step problems reduce to identifying invariant quantities—constant rates of change \(m = \dfrac{\Delta y}{\Delta x}\), conservation of total work/mass, or linear system rank conditions. A two-variable linear system \(a_1 x + b_1 y = c_1\), \(a_2 x + b_2 y = c_2\) has a unique intersection if \(\dfrac{a_1}{a_2} \ne \dfrac{b_1}{b_2}\), no solution (parallel lines) if \(\dfrac{a_1}{a_2} = \dfrac{b_1}{b_2} \ne \dfrac{c_1}{c_2}\), and infinitely many solutions if all three ratios coincide.

label.en: Theorem 1.1 — Modular Arithmetic, Cyclicity, and Repeating Decimals

body.en:
Essential theorems for standardized exam number theory:
  • Modular Arithmetic Compatibility: If \(a \equiv c \pmod m\) and \(b \equiv d \pmod m\), then:
    \[ a + b \equiv c + d \pmod m, \qquad a \cdot b \equiv c \cdot d \pmod m, \qquad a^k \equiv c^k \pmod m \]
  • Units Digit Cyclicity: Powers of integers repeat units digits with periods dividing 4: \(2^n\) (2, 4, 8, 6), \(3^n\) (3, 9, 7, 1), \(7^n\) (7, 9, 3, 1), \(8^n\) (8, 4, 2, 6). To find the units digit of \(a^N\), compute \(N \pmod 4\).
  • Repeating Decimal to Fraction: For a repeating decimal with period \(k\):
    \[ 0.\overline{d_1 d_2 \dots d_k} = \frac{d_1 d_2 \dots d_k}{10^k - 1} = \frac{d_1 d_2 \dots d_k}{99\dots9} \]
  • Sequence Formulas:
    Arithmetic: \(a_n = a_1 + (n - 1)d\), \(S_n = \frac{n}{2}(2a_1 + (n-1)d)\).
    Geometric: \(a_n = a_1 r^{n-1}\), \(S_n = \frac{a_1(1-r^n)}{1-r}\), \(S_\infty = \frac{a_1}{1-r}\) for \(|r| < 1\).

label.en: ▲ ACT Math 2 Traps & Pitfalls — Number Theory

body.en:
• Powers of \(i\) Cycle Modulo 4: \(i^1 = i\), \(i^2 = -1\), \(i^3 = -i\), and \(i^4 = 1\). To evaluate \(i^k\), find \(k \pmod 4\): remainder 1 gives \(i\), remainder 2 gives \(-1\), remainder 3 gives \(-i\), and remainder 0 gives \(1\).
  • Complex Fraction Rationalization: To simplify \(\dfrac{a+bi}{c+di}\), multiply both numerator and denominator by the complex conjugate \(c - di\). The denominator becomes the real number \(c^2 + d^2\).
  • Infinite Geometric Series Convergence: The sum formula \(S_\infty = \dfrac{a_1}{1 - r}\) is strictly valid ONLY when \(|r| < 1\). If \(|r| \ge 1\), the series diverges and has no finite sum.
  • GCD vs. LCM Relationship: Remember the product identity \(\text{GCD}(a,b) \times \text{LCM}(a,b) = a \times b\). If a question asks for the LCM given prime factorizations, take the highest power of each distinct prime; for GCD, take the lowest common power.

label.en: ◆ Why It Works — First-Principles Derivation (Advanced Number Theory)

body.en:
Why Successive Multipliers & Harmonic Average Speed Work: If a quantity \(Q_0\) undergoes a percentage change \(p\%\) followed by \(q\%\), the compound multiplier is the product of individual scale factors:

\[ Q_{\text{final}} = Q_0\left(1 + \frac{p}{100}\right)\!\left(1 + \frac{q}{100}\right) = Q_0\left(1 + \frac{p + q}{100} + \frac{pq}{10000}\right) \]

Notice the cross term \(\dfrac{pq}{10000}\): an increase of \(p\%\) followed by a decrease of \(p\%\) yields \(Q_0\bigl(1 - (p/100)^2\bigr) < Q_0\). Similarly, traveling equal distance \(d\) at speeds \(v_1\) and \(v_2\) takes total time \(T = \frac{d}{v_1} + \frac{d}{v_2}\), so average speed is the harmonic mean \(v_{\text{avg}} = \dfrac{2d}{d/v_1 + d/v_2} = \dfrac{2v_1 v_2}{v_1 + v_2}\).

label.en: Worked Example 1.A — Euclidean Algorithm and LCM Computation

body.en:
Find \(\gcd(252, 198)\) and \(\text{lcm}(252, 198)\).

Step-by-step Solution:
  1. Apply the Euclidean Algorithm of successive division:
    \[ 252 = 198(1) + 54 \]\[ 198 = 54(3) + 36 \]\[ 54 = 36(1) + 18 \]\[ 36 = 18(2) + 0 \]The last non-zero remainder is \(\mathbf{18}\), so \(\gcd(252, 198) = 18\).
  2. Prime factorization check:
    \(252 = 2^2 \times 3^2 \times 7\)
    \(198 = 2 \times 3^2 \times 11\)
    \(\gcd = 2^1 \times 3^2 = 18\).
  3. Compute the LCM using \(\text{lcm}(a, b) = \frac{ab}{\gcd(a, b)}\):
    \[ \text{lcm}(252, 198) = \frac{252 \times 198}{18} = 252 \times 11 = \mathbf{2772} \]
The greatest common divisor is \(\mathbf{18}\) and the least common multiple is \(\mathbf{2772}\).

label.en: Worked Example 1.B — Units Digit of Large Exponents via Cyclicity

body.en:
What is the units digit of \(7^{2026} + 3^{2025}\)?

Step-by-step Solution:
  1. Analyze the powers of 7 modulo 10:
    \(7^1 \equiv 7\), \(7^2 \equiv 9\), \(7^3 \equiv 3\), \(7^4 \equiv 1 \pmod{10}\). Cycle length = 4.
    Divide exponent 2026 by 4:
    \[ 2026 = 4(506) + 2 \implies 7^{2026} \equiv 7^2 \equiv 9 \pmod{10} \]
  2. Analyze the powers of 3 modulo 10:
    \(3^1 \equiv 3\), \(3^2 \equiv 9\), \(3^3 \equiv 7\), \(3^4 \equiv 1 \pmod{10}\). Cycle length = 4.
    Divide exponent 2025 by 4:
    \[ 2025 = 4(506) + 1 \implies 3^{2025} \equiv 3^1 \equiv 3 \pmod{10} \]
  3. Sum the units digits:
    \[ 9 + 3 = 12 \equiv 2 \pmod{10} \]
The units digit of \(7^{2026} + 3^{2025}\) is \(\mathbf{2}\).

label.en: Worked Example C — Advanced Number Theory (Hard Application)

body.en:
Problem (Hard): Two positive quantities \( P \) and \( Q \) are in the ratio \( 4 : 6 \), and the smaller quantity equals \( 28 \). Which of the following is equal to the combined total \( r = P + Q \)?

Step-by-Step Solution: With multiplier \( k = 7 \), \( P + Q = (4 + 6) \times 7 = 70 \).

label.en: Worked Example D — Advanced Number Theory (Easy Application)

body.en:
Problem (Easy): A quantity \( P_0 = 1600 \) increases by \( 20\% \) to \( P_1 \) and then decreases by \( 35\% \) to \( P_2 \). Which of the following is equal to the final quantity \( r = P_2 \)?

Step-by-Step Solution: Computing \( 1600 \times (1 + 0.20) \times (1 - 0.35) = 1248 \).

rows.en: The \(25\%\) reduction applies to the larger base \(1.25 Q_0\), not \(Q_0\).
Dividing by a negative number reverses order on the real number line.
Flip the inequality symbol whenever multiplying or dividing by a negative: \(x < -4\).
Computing round-trip average speed as \(\frac{v_1 + v_2}{2}\)
Time spent at the slower speed is longer than time spent at the faster speed.
Use total distance over total time: \(v_{\text{avg}} = \frac{2v_1 v_2}{v_1 + v_2}\).

label.en: ▲ Exam Pacing & Verification Strategy — Advanced Number Theory

body.en: High-Speed Exam Shortcut (ACT International Subject Test — Math 1): When a linear system asks for a combined expression like \(3x + 3y\) rather than \(x\) and \(y\) individually, add or subtract the two equations directly before isolating either variable—this often yields the target expression in a single step.

question.en: The sum of an arithmetic sequence is 150, with first term \(a_1 = 5\) and last term \(a_n = 25\). How many terms are in this sequence, and what is the common difference \(d\)?

solution.en:
Step 1 (Find \(n\)): Use the arithmetic series sum formula:
\[ S_n = \frac{n}{2}(a_1 + a_n) \implies 150 = \frac{n}{2}(5 + 25) = 15n \implies n = \frac{150}{15} = \mathbf{10} \]

Step 2 (Find \(d\)): Use the \(n\)-th term formula with \(n = 10\):
\[ a_{10} = a_1 + 9d \implies 25 = 5 + 9d \implies 9d = 20 \implies d = \mathbf{\frac{20}{9}} \]

Tier 2 (Key Transformation): Apply the key algebraic/geometric step leading toward \(n\).
Tier 3 (Final Verification): Check signs, units, and domain restrictions on your result before opening the full solution below.

question.en: Express the complex number \(z = \dfrac{5 + 2i}{3 - 4i}\) in standard form \(a + bi\), and determine its modulus \(|z|\).

solution.en:
(a) Standard form \(a + bi\): Multiply numerator and denominator by the complex conjugate \(3 + 4i\):
\[ z = \dfrac{(5 + 2i)(3 + 4i)}{(3 - 4i)(3 + 4i)} = \dfrac{15 + 20i + 6i + 8i^2}{3^2 - (4i)^2} = \dfrac{15 + 26i - 8}{9 - (-16)} = \dfrac{7 + 26i}{25} = \mathbf{\frac{7}{25} + \frac{26}{25}i} \]

(b) Modulus \(|z|\): Using the quotient property \(|z_1/z_2| = |z_1|/|z_2|\):
\[ |5 + 2i| = \sqrt{5^2 + 2^2} = \sqrt{29}, \qquad |3 - 4i| = \sqrt{3^2 + (-4)^2} = \sqrt{25} = 5 \]\[ |z| = \mathbf{\frac{\sqrt{29}}{5}} \approx 1.077 \]

Tier 2 (Key Transformation): Apply the key algebraic/geometric step leading toward \(a + bi\).
Tier 3 (Final Verification): Check signs, units, and domain restrictions on your result before opening the full solution below.

question.en: Convert the repeating decimal \(x = 0.4\overline{36} = 0.4363636\dots\) into an irreducible rational fraction \(\frac{p}{q}\).

solution.en:
Let \(x = 0.4\overline{36}\). Multiply by powers of 10 to shift the non-repeating and repeating parts:
\[ 10x = 4.\overline{36} \]\[ 1000x = 436.\overline{36} \]
Subtract the first equation from the second to eliminate the repeating tails:
\[ 1000x - 10x = 436.\overline{36} - 4.\overline{36} \implies 990x = 432 \]\[ x = \frac{432}{990} \]
Divide numerator and denominator by their greatest common factor (18):
\[ 432 \div 18 = 24, \qquad 990 \div 18 = 55 \implies x = \mathbf{\frac{24}{55}} \]

hints.en: Tier 1 (Conceptual Setup): Identify the governing relationship in Advanced Number Theory and start from \(x = 0.4\overline{36} = 0.4363636\dots\).
Tier 2 (Key Transformation): Apply the key algebraic/geometric step leading toward \(x = 0.4\overline{36}\).
Tier 3 (Final Verification): Check signs, units, and domain restrictions on your result before opening the full solution below.

question.en: An infinite geometric series has first term \(a_1 = 36\) and converges to \(S_\infty = 48\). What is the common ratio \(r\), and what is the third term \(a_3\)?

solution.en:
Using the infinite geometric sum formula \(S_\infty = \frac{a_1}{1 - r}\):
\[ 48 = \frac{36}{1 - r} \implies 1 - r = \frac{36}{48} = \frac{3}{4} \implies r = 1 - \frac{3}{4} = \mathbf{\frac{1}{4}} \]
Since \(|r| = \frac{1}{4} < 1\), the convergence condition holds.
Find the third term \(a_3 = a_1 r^2\):
\[ a_3 = 36 \left(\frac{1}{4}\right)^2 = 36 \times \frac{1}{16} = \mathbf{\frac{9}{4}} = 2.25 \]

hints.en: Tier 1 (Conceptual Setup): Identify the governing relationship in Advanced Number Theory and start from \(a_1 = 36\).
Tier 2 (Key Transformation): Apply the key algebraic/geometric step leading toward \(S_\infty = \frac{a_1}{1 - r}\).
Tier 3 (Final Verification): Check signs, units, and domain restrictions on your result before opening the full solution below.
